stated.value: Best spectroscopy method and exact sensor configuration immediately
What information and first experiment should come before the decision

missing: Process chemistry: composition, solvent or matrix, pH, and typical concentration ranges of the main components
Specification limits and which measured property is out of spec when excursions occur
Candidate contaminants or classes of contaminant, and the concentration at which the process is considered off spec
Detection limit or accuracy required for the quality variable
Frequency, duration, and pattern of off-spec events, and whether they correlate with raw material lots, shifts, or upstream steps
Existing reference lab methods and their precision, plus availability of retained on-spec and off-spec samples
Optical properties of the liquid: colour, turbidity, particulates, bubbles, and fluorescence tendency
Process conditions: temperature, pressure, flow rate, pipe diameter, and the range of each
Access points for a probe or flow cell, and whether a bypass or sample loop is possible
Wetted-material compatibility, cleaning regime (CIP), and sterility or hygiene requirements
Hazardous-area classification and electrical or fibre routing constraints
Required response time and whether the measurement must be closed-loop or only alarm-level

status_reason: The contaminant and the affected quality variable are both unknown, so no spectroscopy method or sensor configuration can be justified yet. Choosing one now would be a guess, and the assessment would not be valid without a spec limit, reference data, and optical properties of the liquid.
answer: An exact sensor configuration cannot responsibly be recommended until the quality variable and the contaminant are identified. The first step is a laboratory study: collect retained on-spec and off-spec samples, identify the variable and contaminant with reference chemistry, and screen those samples with broad-range UV-Vis, NIR, and Raman to see which method discriminates them. The in-line method, probe, and fibre can then be chosen from that evidence.

inline.headline: Identify the contaminant and quality variable in the lab before choosing any in-line spectroscopy
inline.method: Lab phase: reference chemistry (for example HPLC, GC-MS, ICP-MS or OES, Karl Fischer, as relevant) on archived on-spec and off-spec samples, plus broad-range UV-Vis, NIR, and Raman screening of the same samples. The in-line method is selected only after this phase.
inline.probe: No probe is specified yet. Provisional concept only: a flow cell or immersion probe in transmission or ATR geometry, with the path length or ATR crystal selected once the absorbance or Raman response of the target is known.
inline.install: No permanent installation until the target and spec limits are defined. A bypass or sample-conditioning loop with a flow cell is the likely first trial configuration, so that the process is not disturbed.
inline.fiber: Not final. Silica fibre suits UV-Vis and NIR; low-OH fibre is preferred for NIR. Raman needs low-fluorescence fibre with filtering and is sensitive to fibre background, so fibre type depends on the chosen method and the wavelength range.
inline.test_against: Retained on-spec and off-spec samples and reference lab results for the quality variable and contaminant, measured over the full normal operating range and including the excursion conditions.
inline.not_final_because: The contaminant and quality variable are unknown, there are no spec limits or detection-limit requirements, no reference data exist, and the optical properties of the liquid and the process conditions are not known. Any exact configuration now would rest on assumptions that the lab study could easily overturn.

problems.text: An exact sensor configuration cannot be specified while the analyte and quality variable are unknown. Any method chosen now is effectively a guess and may not respond to the contaminant at all.

Contamination is suspected but not confirmed. Off-spec events may come from raw material variation, process drift, temperature or dosing errors, or measurement error, and the spectroscopy strategy differs for each of these.

Optical accessibility of the liquid must be checked before choosing a method. Colour, turbidity, particles, bubbles, or strong fluorescence can make transmission measurements fail and change the choice of probe and method.
Process conditions (temperature, pressure, flow, hazardous area) and wetted-material compatibility with cleaning regimes limit probe type, materials, and installation point.
Without retained off-spec samples or a reliable reference method, no calibration or discrimination model can be validated, and an in-line reading would have no ground truth.

methods.method: Reference chromatography and elemental analysis (HPLC, GC-MS, ICP-MS or OES, Karl Fischer, as relevant)
methods.why: Identifies the contaminant and quantifies the quality variable. It is the ground truth for every later spectroscopic calibration and is not an in-line method.

Robust, fibre-compatible, and well suited to in-line liquid monitoring of bulk composition. It is useful if the contaminant changes overtone or combination bands of the matrix, but it is weak for trace species and needs multivariate calibration.

Gives specific molecular fingerprints and works through glass or polymer windows. It is good for discriminating chemical species and is less affected by water than mid-infrared. Fluorescence and fibre background can limit it, and it is weak for trace species without enhancement.
Simple, low-cost, and fast, with a good detection limit for chromophoric contaminants or colour changes. It is blind to non-absorbing species and sensitive to turbidity and particles.

Relevant only if the contaminant or the quality variable is fluorescent (for example aromatic or conjugated species). It is highly sensitive but non-specific and is strongly affected by matrix and inner-filter effects.

Strong fundamental bands give good chemical specificity. The ATR crystal is prone to fouling in process streams, and the high water absorbance limits aqueous applications, so it is mainly a lab or at-line reference tool at this stage.
Designed for solids, gases, or elemental analysis at surfaces; not a practical first choice for an in-line liquid process with an unknown molecular contaminant.

questions.q: What is the composition of the process liquid, and what are its normal concentration ranges?
questions.why: Defines the background matrix against which a contaminant must be detected and whether it is a bulk or trace change.

questions.q: Which measured property is out of spec, and what are the limits?
questions.why: Determines the quality variable the sensor must predict and the accuracy it needs.

questions.q: What contaminants are suspected, even as a short list or class (for example, metals, organics, microbes, particulates, water)?
questions.why: Narrows the wavelength region, the reference methods, and the method choice.

questions.q: At what contaminant level does the process go off spec, and what detection limit or accuracy is required?
questions.why: Determines whether trace-sensitive methods (fluorescence, enhanced Raman) are needed or whether bulk NIR is enough.

questions.q: Are retained on-spec and off-spec samples available, and how many, from which dates and lots?
questions.why: Without them, no calibration or discrimination model can be built or validated.

questions.q: How often do excursions occur, and do they correlate with raw material lots, shifts, upstream changes, or specific events?
questions.why: Helps separate contamination from other causes and guides where to sample.

questions.q: What is the optical appearance of the liquid (colour, turbidity, particles, bubbles), and is it fluorescent?
questions.why: Determines whether transmission or ATR geometry is viable and whether UV-Vis or fluorescence will be disturbed.

questions.q: What are the process temperature, pressure, flow rate, and pipe size, and their normal ranges?
questions.why: Governs probe rating, flow cell design, and whether a bypass loop is needed.

questions.q: Where can a probe or flow cell be installed, and is a bypass or sample loop permitted?
questions.why: Defines the sampling point, its representativeness, and the response time.

questions.q: What are the wetted-material, CIP, sterility, and hazardous-area constraints?
questions.why: Limits the probe materials, window options, and whether fibre-optic or remote electronics can be used.

questions.q: What response time and output does the process need (alarm only, trend, or closed loop)?
questions.why: Determines acquisition speed, the need for real-time models, and the level of validation required.

experiment.objective: Identify the contaminant and the quality variable responsible for off-spec events, and determine which spectroscopic method (alone or in combination) can detect them at the required level, before any in-line hardware is specified.
steps: Assemble a sample set of retained on-spec and off-spec material, covering all available lots and excursion events, and record the process history for each sample.

Run reference chemistry (for example chromatography, mass spectrometry, elemental analysis, Karl Fischer, or the existing QC method) to identify the contaminant and quantify the quality variable. Compare on-spec and off-spec groups statistically.
Measure all samples on a benchtop UV-Vis, NIR, and Raman system in a flow or cuvette arrangement similar to the process, using the same temperature and dilution where possible.
Check for fluorescence, turbidity, and particle effects, and note which spectral regions carry the difference between on-spec and off-spec samples.

If a difference is found, build a simple calibration or classification model (PLS, PCA with discriminant analysis, or Beer-Lambert for single analytes) with cross-validation on a held-out subset, and report prediction error against the spec tolerance.
Spike known amounts of the suspected contaminant into on-spec material to establish linearity, detection limit, and selectivity against the normal matrix variation.
Only if a method passes the go/no-go criteria, define a short in-line trial with a flow cell or bypass loop, and compare its readings with grab samples taken during the trial.
Document the results and decide the probe, fibre, and installation specification from the evidence.
references: Workman J. and Springsteen A. (eds.), Applied Spectroscopy: A Compact Reference for Practitioners, Academic Press, 1998.
Pelletier M. J. (ed.), Analytical Applications of Raman Spectroscopy, Blackwell Science, 1999.
ASTM E131, Standard Terminology Relating to Molecular Spectroscopy.
ICH Q2(R2), Validation of Analytical Procedures (for method validation principles, where applicable).
experiment.go_no_go: Go to in-line selection only if all of the following hold: (1) the contaminant and the quality variable are identified by reference chemistry; (2) at least one spectroscopic method separates on-spec from off-spec samples, with cross-validated prediction error below the spec tolerance across the normal process range; (3) the required detection limit is shown by spiking; and (4) a probe location and installation that is safe, cleanable, and representative are identified. No-go if no method discriminates at the required level; in that case, return to root-cause investigation of the process rather than adding sensors.

multispectral.combination: Screen NIR and Raman together on the same samples as the first pair, and add UV-Vis plus fluorescence only if the contaminant is chromophoric or fluorescent. Combine methods by data fusion only after each has been shown to work on its own.
multispectral.why: NIR and Raman are complementary: NIR responds to bulk matrix bands and is robust in process conditions, while Raman gives specific molecular fingerprints that can identify a contaminant the matrix hides. Testing them on identical samples shows which one, or which pair, gives the discrimination needed, without committing to hardware in advance.

assumptions: The liquid is sufficiently transparent or can be diluted or conditioned to be measured in transmission or ATR geometry.
Retained off-spec samples exist or can be obtained during the next excursion, and they are representative of the process.
The contaminant is a molecular species or a bulk-property change that spectroscopy can detect, rather than a particulate or microbial problem that requires a different technique.
Reference lab methods are available and accurate enough to serve as ground truth.
No hazardous-area or sterility constraints rule out a flow cell or fibre-optic probe, unless the site information shows otherwise.
The process is not expected to change significantly during the lab study, so that the samples represent the current operation.
